newsitem.title: USA: New documents show Clinton fund-raising frenzy.
newsitem.headline: New documents show Clinton fund-raising frenzy.

text.p: The White House released a second batch of papers belonging to former aide Harold Ickes on Wednesday that document the intense pressure on President Bill Clinton to raise money for his 1996 re-election campaign.

The 6-inch stack of more than 2,000 pages show that anxiety within the party grew so acute in late 1995 that party officials pressed Clinton, Vice President Al Gore and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton to telephone donors directly, a practice the president dislikes and cannot recall doing.

They also show the White House, while consistently denying it solicited donors at more than 100 coffees held at the White House, which would be illegal, typically set and reached $400,000 fund-raising targets for the events.

The documents followed a batch released by the White House in February which showed how intimately involved Clinton was in the effort, including a proposal to invite donors to spend a night at the White House, which the president endorsed in a scribbled note saying: "ready to start overnights right away."

The documents all belong to Ickes, Clinton's former deputy chief of staff who left the administration this year, and have been turned over to a congressional committee investigating campaign fund-raising in last year's presidential election.

They provide a new and stark look at how worried the party became after the Republicans' strong showing in the 1994 congressional elections, in which they captured control of both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years.

One document showed that for the first 10 months of 1996, 117 fund-raising events were scheduled for Clinton, 54 for Gore and 29 for their two wives combined. The party aimed to raise more than $130 million during the 10-month period.

Another memo from February 1996 that Ickes wrote to Clinton and Gore said fund raising would require a "very substantial" commitment from them and their wives and bluntly asked: "Are they willing to commit that amount of time?"

And a late 1995 memo from party officials to Ickes argued that Clinton and Gore should make direct telephone calls and attend a string of fund-raising events to raise $3.2 million for paid television advertising. Clinton has said he does not remember making calls, although he could not rule it out, while Gore has said he made "a few" from the White House.

"Because of the short lead time and lack of time to cultivate additional donors, we believe the following represents the maximum that can be raised prior to year end," said the memo dated Nov. 20, 1995.
The memo then listed a series of proposed activities by Clinton, referred to by his White House acronym POTUS, or President of the United States, and Gore, listed as VPOTUS.

These included "18-20 calls by POTUS" and "10 calls by VPOTUS" as well as a lunch and dinner attended by Clinton, two unspecified events attended by Gore, two by first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and an unspecified "White House Dinner" adding up to $3.2 million for the re-election effort.

A second memo dated Nov. 28, 1995, from Ickes to Clinton and Gore raised the ante, saying that a top party fund-raiser believed a greater effort would be required, including some 20 phone calls by Clinton, 15 by Gore and 10 by the first lady.
White House officials said that Hillary Clinton did not remember having made any such calls.

Lanny Davis, the White House spokesman on the fund-raising controversy, told reporters several hundred pages had been excised from those papers made public, among them papers removed by Ickes' lawyers because they were not "responsive" to the committee's questions and others omitted because of the Democratic Party's concerns about the privacy of its donors.

"I don't think there's anything that you could call new news here," Davis said. "It clearly completes the story that this president and this White House were actively engaged in a very competitive campaign in 1996 with a heavily financed Republican Party outspending us by over $200 million."
He added, "At the end of the day , there is neither anything inappropriate or particularly unusual about a White House during an election year engaged in that kind of legal and appropriate activity."
Asked why people should accept his assertion there was nothing untoward in the fund-raising effort given the many documents omitted, he replied: "I wish I could be sure too."
